items.content: Extract a shared src/shared/mcp-core.ts, byte-identical across context-keeper-remote / agentsync-remote / cambium-remote, guarded by a sha-256 drift test that all three repos pin to the same constant. A published package is the intended end state but deliberately deferred.
items.why: True sharing across three SEPARATE GitHub repos requires either a monorepo, a published npm package, or a git subtree — each of which needs an npm scope, a release workflow, and a coordinated version bump across three independent Cloudflare deploy pipelines. Doing that in the same pass as a batch of security fixes would have coupled an urgent, reviewable change to a risky infrastructure migration. Instead the code was collapsed into ONE import-free file (no imports, so it drops into any repo regardless of their differing extensionless-vs-.js module resolution) that is copied byte-identically, plus a test in each repo that hashes the file's LF-normalized bytes and compares against a constant pinned to the SAME value in all three. Editing the shared file in one repo turns that repo's suite red until the constant is updated, and updating the constant in only one repo makes the divergence visible in review. That converts drift from silent to loud, which was the actual failure mode, and it is reversible in one step once the package exists.  Problem: Three remote MCP Workers each carried their own copy of the JSON-RPC envelope, the MCP handshake semantics, and a safeEqual token comparison. All three safeEqual copies carried the identical comment "kept in sync with the sibling Worker" and all three had nonetheless drifted to different behaviour within six weeks of first shipping: context-keeper-remote percent-decoded the path segment before comparing and the other two did not, and two of the three echoed the client's requested protocolVersion verbatim instead of validating it. A fourth Worker was foreseeable, so the copies had to be collapsed before the drift compounded further.

items.content: The remote Worker serves a read-only phone view at GET /view/<VIEW_TOKEN> -- server-rendered HTML, glance-shaped, on a SEPARATE credential from the MCP connector token -- and enriches it with cambium-remote's team/org knowledge counts via an optional CAMBIUM_STATUS_URL, fail-soft. VIEW_TOKEN unset means the route 404s, and each route refuses the other's token.
items.why: A second, lower-value credential is the whole design. VIEW_TOKEN sits on a GET-only route that issues nothing but SELECTs, so a leaked glance-URL discloses decision summaries rather than write access to 34 projects. The separation is enforced in BOTH directions and tested as such -- /view rejects AUTH_TOKEN and /mcp rejects VIEW_TOKEN -- because a second credential that silently accepts the first is not a second credential. An unset VIEW_TOKEN 404s exactly like any unknown path, so the feature is off until deliberately enabled. Server-rendered rather than a client fetching JSON: the token never reaches JavaScript, there is no CORS surface, and the page works with scripting disabled. One document with inline CSS and zero external references -- on mobile data that is the difference between glanceable and not. Two D1 queries total rather than a fan-out per project. Entry text is arbitrary recorded prose being injected into HTML, so it is escaped and a test proves an summary renders inert. The cambium knowledge panel crosses a NETWORK boundary to a second Worker, so it is treated as an enrichment and never a dependency: bounded at 2.5s, kicked off before the D1 queries so the round trip overlaps rather than adds, and every failure mode (unset secret, timeout, non-200, unexpected shape) degrades to a stated absence rather than a blank space or a hung page. It sends an explicit User-Agent because context-keeper's con-007 records Cloudflare bot rules 403-ing a default client UA -- here that would present as a silently empty panel rather than an error. It shows team and org only: local scope is desktop-only by design AND is the staging area rather than the part that gets read (136 promoted items carry 774 recalls; 229 local ones carry 117), so the page states the absence instead of implying the counts are everything. cambium-remote's status performs no writes and its recall deliberately does not increment recall counters, so glancing from a phone cannot perturb the promotion signals the desktop side reasons about. Problem: The decision logs were only reachable from a desktop MCP client, and glancing at them on a phone had no path. The data was already remote (D1 holds 34 projects / 414 entries via the mirror), so the gap was presentation, not plumbing. But the obvious implementation -- reuse the connector URL -- is dangerous in a specific way this repo has already measured: AUTH_TOKEN is embedded in the URL and is read/write over every project, and the security section documents connector URLs appearing in ~54 places across 13 local transcripts on ONE machine. A dashboard URL is opened on a phone, where it lands in browser history, tab sync and screenshots, so reusing that token would place a full-write credential exactly where it leaks most, and rotating it to recover would break every claude.ai connector simultaneously.

items.content: Never set a Worker secret by passing its value as a command argument, by echoing it into a pipe, or by printing it for a human to copy. Generate it in-process, write it to wrangler's STDIN, hand it off via the clipboard, and display only a masked form. Verify by probing the route for a 200, never by rendering the value back. Two exceptions, both required to be commented where they occur: handing the URL to a browser (no stdin path exists, and the browser holds it in argv and history regardless -- must be opt-out), and a mode-600 file when no clipboard exists (access-controlled, unlike scrollback).
items.why: All three obvious ways to set a secret defeat the reason for having a separate credential. A value passed as argv is visible in the process list to every other user on the machine for the lifetime of the call, and lands in shell history. An echoed value lands in shell history too. A printed value lands in terminal scrollback, in any screen-share or screenshot, and in the transcript of any coding agent that ran the command. That last route is measured, not theoretical: this project's own README documents connector URLs found in ~54 occurrences across 13 local session transcripts on a single machine, none pasted deliberately. VIEW_TOKEN exists precisely so a read-only viewer is not also a write credential; leaking it during setup gives back the separation the design bought. The exceptions are narrow on purpose: each was reached only after confirming no stdin-shaped alternative exists, and each is strictly less exposed than the scrollback it replaces.

items.content: In Windows PowerShell 5.1, never use 2>&1 on a native command while $ErrorActionPreference is 'Stop'. Route native calls through a helper that drops the preference to 'Continue' for the duration of the call and restores it in a finally block.
items.why: 5.1 does not merely merge streams for a native command: it wraps each stderr line in an ErrorRecord, and under 'Stop' the first record is a terminating error. The exit code is irrelevant -- a process that returns 0 still kills the script if it wrote a single line to stderr. Tools that print progress, banners, or update notices to stderr are therefore fatal to any script that redirects them, and the failure is deeply misleading: the error text shown is the tool's own benign warning, so it reads as the tool having failed rather than as a redirection bug in the caller.

items.content: The view is enrolled once by token URL and used thereafter by a long-lived HttpOnly cookie, installed as a PWA. The cookie carries the same VIEW_TOKEN and is compared the same way, so there is exactly one revocation path and no server-side session state.
items.why: Enrol-then-cookie moves the credential from the person to the device, which is what devices are for, without inventing an identity system. Reusing VIEW_TOKEN as the cookie value rather than minting a session id is the key property: revocation stays exactly one action (rotate the secret) and takes effect on the next request for every device at once. A session table would have created a second revocation path, and the one that gets forgotten is the one that stays valid. It also means no D1 writes, no expiry bookkeeping, and no state that can drift from the secret it represents. The PWA manifest points start_url and scope at the tokenless /view, so the installed icon is not a bookmark to a secret.  Problem: Shipping /view/<VIEW_TOKEN> made the credential the user's problem. It is 43 characters, Cloudflare stores secrets write-only so it cannot be read back, and losing the clipboard meant re-running setup and invalidating the URL. For a page whose entire purpose is a ten-second glance on a phone, the handling cost exceeded the value of the thing being protected. The user's verdict was direct: it should be install-once, no keys, no passwords, nothing to remember.

items.content: A runnable command handed to someone must assume nothing about their shell or their working directory. Use forward slashes even on Windows, and either an absolute path or an explicit cd -- never a bare npm run, and never a backslash path.
items.why: Two failure modes, and both look like a broken program rather than a bad instruction. (1) Backslash is an escape character in bash -- Git Bash, WSL, and the shell behind most run-this buttons -- so scripts\set-view-token.cmd collapses to scriptsset-view-token.cmd and reports command not found, naming a file nobody wrote. (2) npm run requires the repo as cwd; from one directory up it emits npm error enoent Could not read package.json, which PowerShell then wraps in a NativeCommandError whose first line is 'At line:1 char:1'. That header mentions no directory and no package.json, so it reads as the script having crashed. In both cases the program never executes, so there is no output and no log, and every diagnostic that assumes it ran is chasing nothing.

items.content: Never test a PowerShell Read-Host result directly against -match or -notmatch. Cast to [string] first, and refuse the destructive path outright when [Environment]::UserInteractive is false. A confirmation must fail closed.
items.why: Read-Host returns $null at EOF, which is every piped, redirected, scheduled, or otherwise non-interactive run. In PowerShell $null -notmatch 'pattern' evaluates to EMPTY rather than $true, so the natural guard if ($answer -notmatch '^[Yy]') { cancel } is falsy on $null and execution falls straight through into the action it was meant to gate. The prompt therefore defaults to yes precisely when no human is present to have said it. Casting to [string] turns $null into the empty string, which the regex correctly fails to match; the UserInteractive check is the belt to that, so the destructive path is unreachable without an explicit flag.

items.content: cambium-remote gained GET /status/<STATUS_TOKEN>, a status-only credential, and the phone view wires to that rather than to cambium's connector URL. Because the token is generated rather than looked up, a script installs it on both Workers with nothing for a human to paste.
items.why: A second, narrower credential solves the security problem and the automation problem with one mechanism. STATUS_TOKEN grants exactly one read -- the counts -- and cannot call recall or reach the knowledge itself, so the blast radius of the thing now stored in two places is three integers rather than an account's entire promoted knowledge. Because it is generated rather than discovered, a script can mint it, install it on cambium-remote, verify the route answers, and only then install the derived URL on the consumer. Rotation is re-running the script, and it is invisible to every MCP client because it is not the connector token. This is the same shape as VIEW_TOKEN in dec-002 and for the same reason: a surface that needs less access should hold a credential that grants less.  Problem: The Knowledge tab needed CAMBIUM_STATUS_URL, and the only way to supply it was to paste cambium-remote's connector URL out of claude.ai. That URL is cambium-remote's AUTH_TOKEN, which grants recall over every promoted item in the team and org scopes, on the Worker whose team scope reaches every repo under TEAM_OWNER including private ones. Rendering three integers on a phone would have copied a full-access credential into a second Worker, so a leak of the second would disclose the reach of the first. It also could not be automated at all: Cloudflare stores secrets write-only, so AUTH_TOKEN can only ever be re-typed by hand, which is exactly the manual credential handling these setup scripts exist to eliminate.

items.content: connect-cambium deploys cambium-remote itself when the status route is missing, rather than telling the operator to. That removes cambium-remote's broken CI from the critical path; repairing that CI is a separate, optional script.
items.why: wrangler is already authenticated on the machine running the script -- it is the same login being used to write secrets on both Workers -- so deploying is available at zero additional credential cost. Doing it there converts a blocking prerequisite into a step the tool handles, and makes the feature independent of a CI pipeline it does not otherwise need. It is scoped tightly: it fires only when the route has already failed to answer for 60 seconds, it deploys that repo's own checked-out main and nothing of this repo's, and -SkipDeploy opts out. Repairing the CI is then genuinely optional, which is the correct priority -- auto-deploy on push is a convenience, while the Knowledge tab working is the actual goal.  Problem: The Knowledge tab could not be wired because cambium-remote had never been deployed with its /status route: its GitHub Actions deploy fails on every merge with empty CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN and CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID secrets, and fails green enough that nobody noticed. The setup script detected the missing route and printed "deploy it, then re-run this" -- which is homework, and homework that presupposed knowing the CI was broken. The operator's position was that a setup script exists precisely so none of that lands on them.

items.content: Deployment happens from a git pre-push hook using the local wrangler login, not from GitHub Actions. The Cloudflare API token that CI requires cannot be created by any credential on the machine, so the answer was to stop needing it rather than to automate obtaining it.
items.why: Checking rather than assuming showed the loop genuinely cannot be closed: minting a Cloudflare API token through the API requires an existing token carrying User API Tokens: Edit, and wrangler's OAuth session holds 29 scopes covering workers, d1, pages, queues and account:read with nothing token-management related. Since no credential on the machine can create that credential, automating the paste is impossible and the real move is to remove the requirement. A pre-push hook deploys with the login that is already present and already used for every secret write in these scripts, so the credential cost is zero. The pre-push ordering is the substantive part: it deploys first and aborts the push on failure, so origin never receives a commit that could not be deployed -- the exact inverse of the failure it replaces, where CI accepted every merge and deployed none.  Problem: cambium-remote's GitHub Actions deploy fails on every merge with empty CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN and CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID, and fails invisibly enough that main drifted ahead of the running Worker for an unknown period. The obvious repair is to set those secrets, but the operator's requirement was full automation with no manual credential step, and the token half appeared to be an irreducible human action.

items.content: Never confirm a deploy with `gh run list --limit 1`. Filter by workflow (`--workflow=deploy.yml`) and check that the run's headSha matches the commit you expect. A repo with CI and Deploy workflows returns whichever finished last, which is usually CI.
items.why: The unfiltered list is ordered by recency across ALL workflows. CI is faster than Deploy, so it almost always finishes first and appears at the top. Reading that as the deploy result reports success while the deploy is still running or has already failed. The failure is silent and durable: the code is merged, main looks correct, tests pass, and every later diagnosis proceeds on the false premise that the running Worker matches the source. Confirming the headSha as well catches the second version of the same mistake, where the right workflow succeeded but for an earlier commit.

items.content: Never verify a Cloudflare secret immediately after setting it. `wrangler secret put` creates a new Worker version and rolls it out, so for up to a minute some edges still serve the previous version holding the previous value. Poll for at least 60 seconds, and never let the failure message assert a single cause.
items.why: A secret change is a deployment, not a database write. Until the new version reaches a given edge, requests there authenticate against the OLD secret, so a correct new token legitimately returns 404 for a while. A short verification window therefore reports a wrong-credential failure for a credential that is correct, and the natural next step -- redeploying, regenerating, or blaming the route -- chases a problem that does not exist. The message matters as much as the timeout: asserting one cause ("it has not been deployed") is confidently wrong half the time, and a wrong diagnosis printed by the tool itself is followed for far longer than no diagnosis at all.

items.content: A Worker cannot reach another Worker by fetching its workers.dev hostname. Use a service binding. Declare it in BOTH the top-level and the named-environment section, since named environments inherit nothing.
items.why: Cloudflare does not route a Worker subrequest to a workers.dev host: the edge answers 404 and the target Worker never executes. From the calling side that is byte-identical to the target rejecting the credential, so the obvious diagnosis is a wrong or unpropagated token, and every fix aimed there is aimed at nothing. The only signal that distinguishes them is the absence of ANY request in the target's own logs. A service binding dispatches in-process -- no DNS, TLS, or egress -- and the request still arrives at the target's normal handler and is still checked against its secret, so the binding replaces the transport and changes nothing about authorization. Keep a plain-fetch fallback for a target on a custom domain, which is routable, or one in another account where no binding can exist.

items.content: Nothing that names another Worker, another account, or a pinned resource id may appear in the TOP-LEVEL wrangler.toml. That config is what the Deploy to Cloudflare button runs, in an account that has none of those things. Put it under [env.production], and remember named environments inherit nothing.
items.why: The top-level profile exists so a stranger's one-click deploy provisions its own resources: the D1 binding deliberately omits database_id for exactly this reason. A service binding is the opposite kind of declaration -- it names a target by name, and Cloudflare rejects the deploy when that Worker does not exist in the deploying account. So a top-level [[services]] breaks the self-host path for everyone except the maintainer, and breaks it at the button, before the deployer has any context for the error. The inheritance direction compounds it: named environments inherit NOTHING, so a binding placed only at the top level is also silently absent from the env CI actually deploys. Both halves have to be got right, and they fail in opposite directions.

items.content: Never emit or run a bare `wrangler deploy` for a repo that declares named environments. Always pass --env explicitly. Any tool that generates a deploy command must refuse to proceed when environments exist and none was named.
items.why: A bare deploy targets the TOP-LEVEL config, and in these repos the top level is the self-host profile: it omits database_id on purpose so Cloudflare auto-provisions a fresh D1 for each one-click deployer. Running it against the maintainer's Worker therefore rebinds a live, populated Worker to a brand-new EMPTY database. Nothing errors, nothing warns, and the deploy reports success -- the data is still in the old database but the Worker no longer points at it, so the failure presents as total data loss. The blast radius is maximal and the signal is zero, which is why the generating tool has to fail closed rather than warn.

items.content: There is exactly one HTML escaper, in src/html.ts. Never define a second one, and never inline an escape in a template. Every string the view renders comes from the store and must pass through it.
items.why: The escaper is the only thing between a recorded string and the rendered page, and the store holds whatever a project wrote -- including text a future contributor pastes from an untrusted source. Copies of it are not merely duplication: they only have to agree until somebody improves one, and the copy that drifts is the one nobody re-reads, so the divergence surfaces as an XSS hole rather than as a failing test. It must also escape both quote characters, not just the angle brackets, because these templates interpolate into attribute values as well as text nodes -- an href attribute built from an entry id is safe only because the double quote is covered.

items.content: Never screenshot a real store for a public repo. Render from a committed synthetic dataset, and check the source database for stray projects before capturing.
items.why: A screenshot of the live view publishes project names and decision summaries permanently, and it is the easiest kind of leak to miss because it does not look like data: nobody greps a PNG before pushing, no diff shows its contents, and it survives in git history after the file is deleted. The same repo already had to force-remove a proposal file that carried content from a private project and one with no remote at all. Rendering from a committed seed also makes the images reproducible rather than one-off artifacts, which matters because screenshots go stale silently -- the UI they depict changes and nothing fails.
